h1: Why you know a smell but cannot name it and how to fix that
title: Why You Know a Smell but Cannot Name It | Craft Beer School
desc: Why a familiar smell in your beer can be impossible to name, what is going on in the brain and the practice that turns it into a word.
teaser: You know that smell. You have smelt it a hundred times. The word will not come. Here is why and how to fix it.
standfirst: Almost every new taster hits the same wall: a beer smells of something familiar and the name refuses to arrive. It is not a poor nose. Smell and language are badly wired together. The link can be trained.
sections: The tip of the nose problem

You lift a glass of Belgian ale and something jumps out. It is warm, a bit sweet, a bit spicy. You have smelt it in a kitchen. You cannot say what it is. Then someone says clove and it clicks at once.

Researchers sometimes call this the tip of the nose state, after the tip of the tongue feeling with words. It is common. Even experienced tasters struggle to name a smell with no context. Ask most people to identify ordinary kitchen smells from unlabelled jars and they get far fewer right than they expect, even when they are sure they know them.
Why smell and words are poorly connected

Sight and hearing are tightly linked to the language areas of the brain. We spend our lives naming what we see. Smell takes a more direct route to areas tied to memory and emotion. That is why a smell can bring back a place or a person in an instant while the name for the smell itself stays out of reach.

Most of us also never practise naming smells. A child is taught red, blue and green with picture books. Nobody sits a child down with a jar of cardamom and a jar of clove. The words are there. The link from smell to word has simply never been built.
Context does most of the work

Labels change what we can name. Show someone a jar marked banana and they will smell banana in a hefeweizen at once. Remove the label and many will say fruity or sweet and stop. This is useful and dangerous at the same time.

Useful, because a word list or a flavour wheel gives your memory a set of candidates. Running down a short list of fruit, spice, malt and hop words often finds the name in seconds. Dangerous, because a suggested word can plant a smell that is not there. On a panel, write your own words before anyone speaks.
Build the link with real references

The fix is practice with physical references, the same way a trained panel learns. Start with smells you can buy in an Indian kitchen or market:

  • Clove, for the spicy phenol in wheat beers and many Belgian ales.
  • Ripe banana, for isoamyl acetate in hefeweizen.
  • Orange and lime peel, for citrus hops.
  • Jaggery and toasted bread, for caramel and bready malt.
  • Fresh coriander seed, for witbier.
  • Cooked sweetcorn, for dimethyl sulphide (DMS) in pale lager.

Put a small amount of each in a clean jar with a lid. Smell one, say the name out loud, then smell the matching beer. Repeat until the word arrives without the label. Our guide on retronasal smell explains why you should also notice these notes after you swallow.

Once the names come easily with labels, take the labels away. Ask someone to hand you the jars in a random order with the lids taped. Score yourself. With ten minutes a day, most people find their score climbs quickly. The improvement is in recall, not in the nose itself.

Then repeat the test with beer. Smelling clove in a jar is easier than finding it under alcohol, fruit and malt in a Belgian dubbel. A good guided session with spiked samples bridges that gap, because the target compound is added to a real beer at a known level.
Why naming matters beyond the pub

Naming a smell is not a party trick. It is how faults get fixed. A brewer who hears that a lager smells a bit off can do nothing with it. A brewer who hears cooked sweetcorn knows to look at DMS, the boil and wort cooling. A brewer who hears green apple thinks of acetaldehyde and whether the beer left the tank too early.

The same applies at the bar. A drinker who can say buttery rather than strange gives the bar manager something to act on, usually a line that needs cleaning. Clear words turn a vague complaint into a useful report. That is the real payoff from the jar practice above.

The last step is to replace vague words with exact ones. Fruity becomes pear, apricot or green apple. Spicy becomes clove, pepper or coriander. Sweet becomes honey, toffee or bread crust. Specific words are easier to remember, easier to compare across tastings and far more useful to a brewer trying to fix a fault.

A tasting sheet that keeps a running list of the words you have used is a good habit. Over time it becomes your own vocabulary, built from smells you have actually met.

Tonight, put clove, banana and orange peel in three jars. Smell each with its name for a minute. Tomorrow, have someone mix up the jars and see how many you get right. Then open a wheat beer and look for all three.
faqs: Why can I recognise a smell but not name it?
Smell is wired closely to memory and emotion but weakly to the language areas of the brain. Most people also never practise naming smells, so the link stays weak.
How do I get better at naming beer aromas?
Practise with physical references such as clove, banana and citrus peel. Smell each with its name, then test yourself blind and look for the same notes in beer.
Yes, as a list of candidates to jog memory. Write your own words first, though, because a suggested word can make you smell something that is not there.
